title: Manchester City have a Phil Foden problem
content:
It has been a curious season for Phil Foden. Having ended 2025 with a run of six goals in four league games, he has only started two of seven matches since the Manchester derby on January 17.

It should not be forgotten that there appeared to be very good reasons for Foden’s obvious struggles last year, when he dipped well below the level he had shown in 2023-24 as he helped fire Manchester City to the title with a string of fine goals and performances.

“I’ve had a lot of things going on off the pitch mentally,” he told the media last May. “Sometimes there’s things in life bigger than football. This season I’ve struggled a little bit. Hopefully, come next year, I can get my head mentally right.”

There were also physical problems, with an ankle injury proving troublesome, but it is clear that things were far from easy. “If everything was OK (off the pitch), I’d definitely be better on the field,” he also said.

Progress, in that sense, is unlikely to be linear: he had appeared to be back to his best leading up to Christmas, and had told TNT Sports after scoring two fine goals against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League that he was “loving it”. “I need to play with a smile on my face, which I’m doing,” he said.

But he has barely featured this calendar year and, when he has, he has visibly struggled at times.

His appearance in the 2-2 draw with Nottingham Forest on Wednesday evening is another one that falls into that category. While there were many factors in City dropping points, Foden’s role in the visitors’ second goal was certainly one of them.

“It’s quite frustrating today, just because they didn’t create much,” Bernardo Silva told reporters after the match. “Whatever they created, they scored. First goal is an unbelievable goal from Morgan (Gibbs-White). The way he finishes, it’s quite surprising. So I would say in this type of situation, we clap and that’s it.”

Gibbs-White’s goal was a smart backheel that did catch everybody out, but Elliot Anderson’s strike, as good a goal as it was, left a lot to be desired from a City point of view.

“The second action frustrates me a little bit more because we don’t defend well,” Bernardo added. “There’s a clear one-two that we don’t follow the movement, and at the end, when you don’t do the basics, well… you get punished.”

When it was suggested by a journalist that the goal was simply the result of a “sharp” bit of play, Bernardo took exception.

“It’s not sharp enough,” he insisted. “It’s not sharp enough for you to be beaten, so it is what it is. Mistakes happen, we go to the next one, but we need to defend better with those actions.”

Bernardo did not name names, but it is obvious from the footage that it was Foden who was easily bypassed with a one-two, allowing Anderson to pass and move around him with no resistance. Top-level footballers know that in situations like those, they have to obstruct the passing player so they do not have a free run at the return pass. As much as Anderson held up his end of the bargain, it was also made easier for him.

Mistakes, as Bernardo notes, do indeed happen, and on a night when City missed chances and did not always use the ball well, there were plenty of them. But given Foden’s current situation, his error could not have come at a worse time.

“Step by step, he will be back,” Pep Guardiola told reporters a month ago, acknowledging a dip in form that had started to creep in since the start of the year. “He’s my son. He’s our son.

“We try to protect him and get him back to his best. We need his best to come back where we are.

“He’s a human being. Eight or nine years’ career, sometimes you have ups and downs. It’s as simple as that.”

Foden was substituted at half-time of January’s Manchester derby defeat, where, although he damaged a bone in his hand, Guardiola had said that his decision was purely tactical. The 25-year-old did not look happy when he was taken off a few days later during the 3-1 defeat at Bodo/Glimt.

The relationship between the two, though, seemed as strong as ever at Anfield a few weeks later. As the City bench erupted following Erling Haaland’s late winner, Guardiola and Foden hugged each other in a way that a father and son probably would.

That also tells a story in itself: Foden was on the bench at Anfield, as he has been for most Premier League matches over the past six weeks. He was dropped for the game against Wolves, which followed the Bodo defeat, and has been used sparingly since. He did not come on at Anfield, played just two minutes at Tottenham Hotspur, and just three against Newcastle United.

Places in City’s attacking positions have become harder to come by of late. Haaland himself was left out of the game against Wolves, leading Guardiola to return to the 4-2-2-2 shape that he adopted at the end of last season in the Norwegian’s absence.

In that time, Rodri has returned to better health and Nico O’Reilly has impressed in midfield. Bernardo, as has been the case all season, is regarded as indispensable. Haaland and Antoine Semenyo have generally taken the two most advanced positions, leaving just one spot in the ‘middle two’, with Foden, Rayan Cherki and Tijjani Reijnders all fighting for it. There is also Omar Marmoush, who sometimes plays higher when Semenyo is deeper.

Foden has played in cup competitions, with games against Exeter City in the FA Cup and two against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup semi-finals. Wednesday night’s outing, like the game against Fulham on February 11, felt like a relatively rare opportunity for Foden to stake his claim in Guardiola’s plans for the Premier League.

He could not take advantage, though; even before the main defensive error, there were bobbly or misplaced passes that suggested he is not at his sharpest right now.

There are a couple of extra layers of complexity here.

Firstly, Foden’s contract expires at the end of next season. It is inconceivable that he would not get a new one, but negotiations cannot be easy to conduct given the uncertainty over his output, even if City have always been incredibly supportive during his low points.

Then there is the fact that this is a World Cup year. Foden opened up on his off-the-field struggles last May because he had asked to be left out of Thomas Tuchel’s England squad, with the manager saying the forward needed to “re-find the joy in his game”.

Foden did not make the next two England squads, either, but was back in November during his improved form. Tuchel, though, has made a point of generally picking players who are making regular and impressive contributions to their clubs, and it will be interesting to see whether he sticks with Foden when the latest squad is named at the end of March.

These are hefty situations for Foden himself to wrangle with, and while there has been no suggestion that the off-the-pitch battles that took their toll last season have returned, it should be something that is taken into consideration.

City’s setback against Forest comes at a time when they had started to piece back together some good form and results, following a dip in January as they struggled with injury.

Their form has been on an upward trajectory, but even so, an extra spark from that final midfield spot would be very useful, whether it be from Cherki, Reijnders, or Foden.

Considering the highs that Foden has achieved, including the form he had shown before Christmas, and that the other two are new to the league, there is always going to be more expectation on him. Maybe that is part of the problem.
